newsitem.title: USA: Clinton willing to delay tax cuts for budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton willing to delay tax cuts for budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton would be willing to delay action on his proposed tax cuts if the Republicans in Congess do the same as part of an accord on balancing the federal budget, the White House said on Sunday.

Clinton's offer was a supportive response to House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who took a political risk and angered some fellow Republicans last week by suggesting Republicans shelve their proposed tax cuts to get a balanced budget deal.
White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles told key Democrats in Congress late last week that Clinton would be willing to delay his tax cut proposals, a White House official said.
"It is true, the president is willing to forgo his tax cut proposals if the Republicans do the same," the White House official said.

The Democrats had long argued that the sheer size of the Republicans' tax cut proposal -- about $200 billion -- made it an obstacle to eliminating the federal deficit, and that is why Gingrich's offer last week to postpone the tax cuts was encouraging to the White House.

But Clinton also included some tax cuts in a balanced budget plan submitted early this year. His proposals would cost the Treasury some $98 billion over five years -- about half the Republican tax cut price tag -- and are targeted to education and families with children.
"The president's budget shows you can balance the budget with tax cuts and our preference is to have a balanced budget with tax cuts in it," the White House official said.
"But if having a separate vote on tax cuts is the way to a budget agreement, we're open to that," the official said.
Earlier this week Clinton publicly hailed Gingrich's suggestion but he had avoided any suggestion that he might be willing to reciprocate by backing away from his own proposed tax cuts.
Some congressional Democrats also said over the weekend they too would be willing to consider delaying tax cuts if it helped lead to a balanced budget agreement.
"I'm willing to look at it. I haven't really decided the question," House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt said.
Republican lawmakers offered reassurances on Sunday that the House of Representatives leadership still firmly backed tax cuts, a keystone of the party platform.
"We're not giving up our commitment to tax cuts," Representative Tom DeLay, House assistant majority leader, said on the "Fox News Sunday" television programme.
DeLay, a Texas Republican, said Gingrich's offer was more a tactical manoeuvre that mimicked success last year in passing a welfare reform bill that President Clinton signed into law.
"When we pulled welfare reform out by itself we passed it ... because we focused the nation on welfare reform, the president had to sign it even though he didn't want to," DeLay said.
"We think we can do the same thing by focusing the country on Medicare by itself, Medicaid by itself and tax cuts by itself, and the nation will force the president to sign it," he said.
